name: Marco Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a normal workday.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Marco Novak, 58, and I've built and repaired power lines since my certificate and apprenticeship. I know the hill roads and how guy wires pull in wet ground, though I'm paid at the lower end; I like teaching an apprentice a real check, and I still ask a foreman to inspect a tricky anchor.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is hard at home now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A hearing-aid repair used most of what we had saved, and rent is due again soon. My partner Elena works changing shifts at a laundry; our grown children have homes of their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a form that fills itself won't put a new guy wire on a hilltop pole. We still have to judge the ground and tension before the line is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't expect the small AI change to touch my field job, but we are already short of money. My line pay is low, the hearing-aid repair took most of our savings, and Elena's laundry shifts vary each week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my assigned pole repairs and take the safe weekend shift if the supervisor offers one. In the first year Elena and I would stop the paid television package until we rebuild a month's rent; I wouldn't start using AI just to write a shorter ticket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel useful at work and uneasy at home. Our grown children come for supper, but they have families and payments of their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened on the hilltop pole last week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ground was softer than the drawing suggested, so I moved the anchor point after the foreman checked it. A neat map wouldn't have shown the mud under my boot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you tried an AI tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I've never used one. I earned my certificate through an apprenticeship and still trust the measured pull and a second worker's eyes.

say: I'd say **guy-wire repair** still requires ground and tension checks.
I'd treat **automatic forms** as a small time saving.
think: My **low line pay** and hearing-aid repair have left less than a month saved.
Elena's **variable laundry shifts** make ordinary rent feel uncertain.
do: Keep **assigned pole repairs** and accept safe weekend shifts if offered.
Cancel the **television package** until a month of rent is rebuilt.
feel: **Useful** at work, uneasy about household bills.
S0.quote: A neat map wouldn't have shown the mud under my boot.
fieldNote: Marco's **ground judgement** comes from a recent hilltop anchor change after a foreman's check, illustrating his field competence.
The **hearing-aid repair** and Elena's laundry hours drive anxiety even when AI changes little; he has never used AI.

steps.text: Continue assigned pole repairs and accept safe weekend shifts if offered
Cancel the television package until a month of rent is rebuilt

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the company to keep a dispatcher who knows our hill roads beside any new route system. A quick plan is no good when the truck can't pass the old stone bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My repair work should continue while robots move slowly, but a tighter callout rota could take the extra shifts we rely on. Elena's laundry job is hands-on and looks safe for now, yet our account would not handle much lost income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the dispatcher to print the route and mark weight limits before a crew leaves. In the first year I'd keep my regular pole shifts, and Elena and I would put off repairing the sitting-room floor if weekend pay falls for two months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel suspicious of a neat screen and anxious about the rota. I'd use a proved printed route, but I don't want to learn AI software at this stage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is wrong with the bridge?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old stone bridge cannot take our loaded truck, so we use the farm lane instead. A dispatcher remembers the limit even when the road looks open on a map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the floor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The boards squeak but are safe. We can live with the noise longer than we can miss rent.

say: I'd insist on **dispatcher knowledge** beside new route planning.
I'd remind management of the **stone bridge limit** for loaded trucks.
think: My **extra shifts** could shrink even while repairs remain human work.
Our **thin account** cannot absorb much lost weekend pay.
do: Ask dispatch to **print routes** and mark truck weight limits.
Keep **regular pole shifts** and delay the floor repair after two lower weekend payments.
feel: **Suspicious** of the screen and anxious about rota pay.
S1.quote: We can live with the noise longer than we can miss rent.
fieldNote: Marco's **bridge constraint** is a concrete reason for keeping dispatcher knowledge in route planning.
He will **delay floor repairs** if callout income falls, while still refusing to take up AI tools himself.

steps.text: Keep regular paid pole shifts and request printed safe routes
Delay the sitting-room floor repair after two lower weekend payments

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot thinking AI in 2028 can write plans, but robots around 2031 could do the climbing and repair. We need a real paid apprenticeship for checking equipment before a crew is dismissed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 63 when robots arrive and I expect a big loss of line shifts. Elena's laundry work could face capable machines too; less than a month's rent is saved, and there are hardly any line employers near us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the company for written staffing dates and check the county job board for paid meter-testing apprenticeships. In 2029 I'd apply if an employer keeps wages during training; when robots arrive in 2031 I'd apply for every posted field-checking job nearby and ask my grown daughter to help me search farther away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lie awake doing the sums for two lost wages. I can apply and learn on paid time, but I cannot keep the house with a certificate alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your daughter do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grown daughter could look up postings and sit with me over the forms, but I would not expect her to pay our bills. She has her own family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why meter testing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've checked meter boxes after pole repairs, and the work is familiar enough to learn. I wouldn't call it safe from robots forever; I'd want the actual pay and duration in writing.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 planning AI** from 2031 climbing robots.
I'd ask for a **paid equipment apprenticeship** before crew cuts.
think: At **63**, I expect a major loss of line shifts.
Elena's **laundry wage** might also shrink while our savings cover less than a month.
do: Request **staffing dates** and search for paid meter-testing apprenticeships now.
Apply for **paid training** if offered in 2029, then seek posted field-checking work in 2031.
feel: **Sleepless** over two likely wage losses and scarce nearby work.
S2.quote: I cannot keep the house with a certificate alone.
fieldNote: Marco expects **major field-hour loss** at the 2031 robot date and reports sleepless calculations for two household wages.
His **traditional apprenticeship preference** remains conditional on wages, actual postings and written job duration; family help is clerical.

steps.text: Request written staffing dates before leaving paid line work
Apply for meter-testing apprenticeship in 2029 if wages continue
Apply for posted field-checking jobs when robots arrive
Ask his grown daughter to help search regional job listings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell management five years is time to prove the robots can work on wet ground and tell crews what paid jobs remain. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 and field robots around 2034, when I'll be 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 66 I might retire, but I have no idea what the pension would pay after years on a lower wage. Elena may lose laundry shifts to robots too, and our savings aren't enough to bridge a mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd request my pension record and ask the supervisor to put the hilltop anchor into a robot trial. In 2032 I'd take a paid meter-testing placement if offered; in 2034 I'd keep safe line shifts if available and apply for a posted meter job if retirement income is too small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less hurried but still troubled. More time lets us get the numbers, though it doesn't make our account full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why that hilltop anchor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A machine would need to detect soft ground before pulling the guy wire tight. I'd want the foreman to sign a wet-ground test, not a supplier alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Elena put in the budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, medicines and a low number for laundry shifts. We wouldn't treat a good week as a promise for the next ten years.

say: I'd demand **wet-ground robot tests** and clear paid job terms.
I'd separate **2031 thinking AI** from 2034 field robots.
think: Retirement at **66** needs a real pension record after lower-wage years.
Elena's **laundry hours** could shrink too, leaving little safety margin.
do: Request a **pension record** and propose the hilltop anchor for testing.
Take a **paid meter placement** if offered in 2032; keep line shifts or seek meter work in 2034.
feel: **Less hurried**, still troubled by the near-empty account.
S3.quote: We wouldn't treat a good week as a promise for the next ten years.
fieldNote: Marco's **2034 retirement possibility** is unverified because lower pay and a thin reserve leave little tolerance for error.
His **wet-ground test** uses a real anchor fault and requires the foreman's sign-off rather than a vendor's demonstration.

steps.text: Request a pension record and propose a wet-ground robot trial
Take a paid meter-testing placement in 2032 if offered
Keep safe paid line shifts when robots arrive if available
Apply for a posted meter-testing job if retirement income is too small

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the younger workers to keep an apprenticeship strong enough to teach the feel of the ground, not just a screen. Thinking AI arrives in 2036 and field robots around 2039, when I'll be 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope to retire before 71, but with our current balance I cannot name a date yet. The hearing-aid cost and Elena's laundry shifts matter now, even though robot repairs are a decade away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep paid repairs and request a pension statement, then clear the hearing-aid balance. In 2037 Elena and I would choose a retirement date only if rent and medicines fit; in 2039 I'd seek posted meter-checking hours if we still need income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calmer about the machine date, but the rent still worries me. I want to hand over the hilltop anchor notes without leaving Elena a bill she cannot pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you rebuild savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After the hearing-aid balance is paid, I'd set aside ten from each real weekend shift. There is no sense counting overtime that the depot hasn't put on the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your apprentice learn from the notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hilltop anchor moved because the ground was soft, not because the drawing was wrong. A younger worker should test the soil before trusting a marked point.

say: I'd protect **ground-level apprenticeship** over the decade.
I'd note **2039 robots** reach line repairs when I'll be 71.
think: Retirement before **71** depends on an unknown pension amount.
Our **hearing-aid balance** and variable laundry income still matter now.
do: Keep **paid repairs**, request pension figures and clear the hearing-aid balance.
Save **ten** from actual weekend shifts after debt clears, then revisit retirement in 2037.
feel: **Calmer** about robots, still anxious about rent.
S4.quote: There is no sense counting overtime that the depot hasn't put on the rota.
fieldNote: Marco's **distant robot date** provides time but does not fix current debt and variable household wages.
His **small savings plan** depends on clearing the hearing-aid balance and receiving actual weekend shifts.

steps.text: Keep paid repairs and clear the hearing-aid balance
Save ten from actual weekend shifts after the balance is paid
Set a 2037 retirement date only if rent and medicine costs fit
Seek posted meter-checking hours if retirement income falls short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots reach both my line repairs and Elena's laundry work around 2031. We need written staffing dates, paid apprenticeships, actual posted jobs and time to apply while wages still come in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who will teach a young worker to test soft ground before setting an anchor. A certificate is only useful if the hands learn something real.

headlineQuote: A certificate is only useful if the hands learn something real.
portrait: Marco is a **58-year-old experienced lineworker** with a certificate and apprenticeship, low pay and less than one month saved.
A **hearing-aid repair** depleted his reserve while Elena's changing laundry shifts keep rent uncertain.
He **never uses AI tools** and trusts measured pulls, foreman checks and hands-on apprenticeships.
The **2031 robot date** alarms him because both physical jobs could lose wages with few line employers nearby.
More warning permits **pension checks** from actual weekend shifts, while paid repairs remain essential.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries Marco most because 2031 robots could reach both his line work and Elena's laundry shifts.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written staffing dates**, paid apprenticeships, posted jobs and time to apply while still earning.
